text: CNN EARLY EDITION
MARCH 22, 2000
SPEAKERS:
DR. DAVID KESSLER, FORMER COMMISSIONER, FDA
LEON HARRIS, CNN ANCHOR
BROADCAST EXCERPT
HARRIS: As FDA commissioner, David Kessler fought for the administration's plan
to regulate tobacco as a drug. He is currently now dean of Yale University School of
Medicine.
And Dr. Kessler joins us from New York this morning with his views on what the
president and Congress should do now.
We thank you for coming in and sharing with us your views on this particular issue. Will
it be easier actually to create a new agency rather than to rely on Congress to actually
do something considering that the Republican leadership is saying right now, is sending
signais that they will not do anything on this matter?
KESSLER: Well, I think that's not a very wise decision for the Republican leadership.
The fact is, if you look at all of the evidence, if you look at all of the evidence we've
uncovered over the last five years of what the tobacco companies have known about
the addictive effects, there is no question that we're dealing with an addictive drug. In
fact, Philip Morris has even said that over the last couple of weeks.
What other addictive drug isn't regulated by the FDA?
HARRIS: But, Dr. Kessler, those Republicans in Congress we just heard speak this
morning have been looking at those very same facts and have been doing so for years,
and their position has not changed. We also no bring into the equation the fact that this
is also an election year.
KESSLER: This does not have to be a campaign issue. This is a public health issue.
Philip Morris has even supported FDA regulation. So I'm puzzled why the Republican
leadership isn't willing to look at this product and see what I think all Americans see, the
fact is that nicotine is an addictive drug, and it should be regulated by the Food and
Drug Administration.
HARRIS: So then, the tobacco companies that you mention now, had in the past said
that they would be willing to accept some regulation. Now do you expect them to back
pedal off of that position since the Supreme Court has opened the door?
KESSLER: No, I don't think so. I mean, if you look at the lay of the land, if you look at
